name: turnip yam pie
instructions:
Vegetable pot pie built on ATK's Vegetable Pot Pie base with several load-bearing modifications: bouillon-based stock (not vegetable broth), porcini mushroom powder in place of parmesan. Named for TURNIPS + SWEET POTATOES ('yams' colloquially) — the two roots are the identity of the dish; cremini mushrooms + swiss chard round it out under a flaky pie crust. GINGER AND LEMON are used interchangeably or together as a brightening axis to balance the earthy roots — not load-bearing on their own, just the balance.

SERVES 4-6. 9 1/2-inch deep-dish pie plate.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

Crust:
- 1 single-crust pie dough (homemade all-butter or store-bought, rolled to a 10-inch circle)
- 1 large egg
- 1 tsp water

Filling:
- 4 tbsp unsalted butter (split: 2 tbsp + 2 tbsp)
- 1 yellow onion, chopped fine
- 8 oz cremini mushrooms, trimmed and quartered if large or halved if small
- salt and pepper
- 12 oz sweet potato (~1 medium), peeled and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
- 8 oz turnips, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/2 tsp grated lemon zest + 1 tbsp lemon juice (part of the brightening axis — see BRIGHTENING AXIS note)
- 8 oz (OR MORE) swiss chard, stemmed and cut into 1-inch pieces — DON'T CHICKEN OUT ON THE AMOUNT, they wilt down (see CHARD note)
- 2 tbsp all-purpose flour
- 2 cups bouillon-based stock (chicken or dark vegetable — NOT beef, NOT plain vegetable broth, NOT garden vegetable bouillon which turns the gravy mossy green; see STOCK note)
- 1 tbsp porcini mushroom powder (or nutritional yeast — replaces the parmesan; see GLUTAMATE note)
- 1 tbsp freshly grated fresh ginger, added off heat at the end (other half of the brightening axis — interchangeable with or additive to the lemon; see BRIGHTENING AXIS note)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREP THE CRUST: roll the pie dough between 2 large sheets of parchment paper into a 10-inch circle. Peel off the top parchment. Fold over the outer 1/2-inch edge of dough, then crimp into a tidy fluted edge with your fingers. Using a paring knife, cut four 2-inch oval-shaped vents in the center. Slide the parchment with the crust onto a baking sheet and refrigerate until needed.
2. Adjust an oven rack to the middle position and preheat to 400°F.
3. SAUTÉ MUSHROOMS + ONION: melt 2 tbsp butter in a dutch oven over medium heat. Stir in the onion, mushrooms, and 1/2 tsp salt. Cook until the mushrooms have released their liquid, about 5 min.
4. ADD ROOT VEGETABLES: stir in the sweet potato and turnips. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the sweet potato and turnips begin to soften around the edges, 7-9 min. Stir in the garlic and lemon zest and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
5. WILT THE CHARD: stir in the swiss chard and cook until wilted, about 2 min. Transfer everything to a bowl.
6. BUILD THE GRAVY: melt the remaining 2 tbsp butter in the now-empty pot over medium-high heat. Stir in the flour and cook for 1 min. Gradually whisk in the bouillon-based stock, scraping up any browned bits and smoothing out any lumps. Bring to a simmer and cook until the sauce thickens slightly, about 1 min. Off heat, whisk in the porcini mushroom powder (or nutritional yeast), lemon juice, and 1/2 tsp salt.
7. RECOMBINE AND ADD BRIGHTENER(S): stir the cooked vegetables back in along with any accumulated juices. Add your brightening axis OFF HEAT — grated fresh ginger (~1 tbsp) and/or extra lemon juice. Use both, either, or one — they're interchangeable brighteners for the earthy roots (see BRIGHTENING AXIS note). Season with salt and pepper to taste.
8. ASSEMBLE: transfer the filling to a 9 1/2-inch deep-dish pie plate set on an aluminum-foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Place the chilled crust on top. Lightly beat the egg, water, and a pinch of salt together in a bowl, then brush over the crust.
9. BAKE until the crust is golden brown and the filling is bubbling, about 30 min. Let cool for 10 min before serving.
notes:
Adapted from America's Test Kitchen's Vegetable Pot Pie (Hearty Vegetable Mains chapter). The ATK original: mushroom + sweet potato + turnip + swiss chard filling, vegetable broth gravy, parmesan whisked in, minced parsley, single pie crust on top. I've kept the vegetable stack and technique but made three load-bearing changes documented below. Renamed to 'turnip yam pie' because the TURNIPS + SWEET POTATOES (colloquially 'yams') are the identity of the dish — the two roots are what carry it. Ginger and lemon are a brightening axis on top, not the identity themselves (see BRIGHTENING AXIS note).

=== STOCK: BOUILLON-BASED, NOT VEGETABLE BROTH ===

ATK calls for vegetable broth. Vegetable broth ISN'T STRONG ENOUGH — the gravy reads watery and background against the earthy roots and mushrooms.

Use bouillon cubes or better-than-bouillon paste dissolved in the 2 cups of liquid: CHICKEN or DARK VEGETABLE. Chicken is my usual pick. BEEF probably won't work — too heavy and iron-forward against the sweet-potato-and-lemon register.

Homemade chicken stock would also work if you have it strong enough.

--- COOK NOTE — GARDEN VEGETABLE BOUILLON TURNED THE GRAVY MOSSY GREEN ---

Last time I made this with a GARDEN VEGETABLE BOUILLON CUBE. Tasted great — flavor was in the right range. BUT once the flour hit the stock and thickened it into gravy, the color turned MOSSY GREEN. Perfectly edible, but visually off — I wouldn't serve it to others in that state.

Next time: DARK VEGETABLE bouillon or CHICKEN bouillon. Both give a golden-brown gravy color that reads normal on the plate. Garden vegetable bouillon has enough herb/green powder in the mix that the tinted broth + roux reads visually mossy rather than golden-savory. Save it for a dish where the visual gets covered.

=== TURNIPS + SWEET POTATOES (YAMS) ARE THE IDENTITY — DON'T SUB EITHER OUT ===

The two roots together are what the dish IS. Turnips bring the earthy, slightly bitter, savory-root character; sweet potatoes bring the sweet/savory counterweight. Together they cover the sweet-earthy axis — one alone leaves the pie half-formed. Don't sub in regular potato for the sweet potato (loses the sweet/savory balance) and don't skip the turnips (loses the earthy backbone).

A note on YAM vs SWEET POTATO naming: in American English 'yam' and 'sweet potato' are colloquially interchangeable — true yams (Dioscorea) are a different genus but almost never what's meant. The 'yam' in the recipe name is the colloquial usage; the actual ingredient is orange-fleshed sweet potato.

=== BRIGHTENING AXIS: GINGER AND/OR LEMON — INTERCHANGEABLE OR TOGETHER ===

The earthy turnip + sweet potato + mushroom base wants something bright on top to balance it. Ginger and lemon are the two brighteners that work here — INTERCHANGEABLE OR TOGETHER. Either alone brightens the dish enough; both together is fine and my usual play.

- LEMON ONLY: ATK's original approach. Zest early (with the garlic), juice late (whisked into the finished gravy). Works.
- GINGER ONLY: freshly grated ginger stirred in at the end (off heat). Also works — pushes the dish slightly more warm/savory-bright than lemon does.
- BOTH: what I usually do. Zest + juice from the lemon per ATK; ~1 tbsp grated ginger stirred in at the end. The two brighteners don't fight each other.

Whichever bright ingredient(s) you use, ADD OFF HEAT — for ginger, top notes are volatile and cook off quickly; for lemon, the acid dulls if it simmers. Off heat at the end is where both belong.

This brightening axis is a balance layer, not the identity — the pie's identity is the two roots. If you're out of both ginger AND lemon, the dish will still work; it just reads a little muddier without the bright top note.

--- FAILURE MODE — TOO MUCH BRIGHTENER (SAUCE REDUCES IN THE OVEN) ---

Easy to overdo the lemon juice, lemon zest, and/or ginger. The trap: when you taste the filling on the stovetop before assembly, it needs to read slightly UNDER-brightened, because the sauce REDUCES during the 30-min bake and concentrates all three brightening flavors. What tasted balanced going in tastes lemon-forward or ginger-forward coming out.

Add LESS THAN YOU THINK YOU NEED — start with the amounts in the ingredient list (1/2 tsp zest, 1 tbsp juice, ~1 tbsp grated ginger), taste, and resist the urge to add more just because it seems 'balanced now.' The oven will do the concentrating.

=== SKIP THE PARMESAN — USE PORCINI POWDER OR NUTRITIONAL YEAST INSTEAD ===

ATK whisks 1 oz grated parmesan into the finished gravy for umami and body. I've been using PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER instead — same umami hit without the dairy weight, and it doubles down on the mushroom character that's already carrying the dish. NUTRITIONAL YEAST would also work here (haven't tested it in this dish yet but it should slot in the same role).

This is one of the times the vegan-glutamate-additions play is exactly right — the pie already has 3+ vegetables carrying real work, and the porcini/nooch reads as extension of the mushrooms rather than a shortcut layer. Cross-reference [[feedback_vegan_glutamate]]: this is the good version of that pattern, not the bad one.

=== SKIP THE PARSLEY ===

ATK finishes with 2 tbsp minced parsley. I've skipped it and don't miss it. The pie doesn't need the herbal green note — the swiss chard is already providing green vegetable weight, and the ginger + lemon are doing the freshness work. Add parsley if you want but it's optional.

=== DON'T CHICKEN OUT ON THE SWISS CHARD ===

The 8 oz called for LOOKS like a lot when raw — a big heap of greens in the pot. I chickened out and used less last time; came out short on chard. THEY WILT DOWN DRAMATICALLY during the 2-min cook — 8 oz raw becomes maybe 1/3 the volume in the finished pie. Use the full amount (or more) and trust the reduction.

=== DON'T USE ASPARAGUS OR LEEKS (ATK'S NOTE, WORTH KEEPING) ===

ATK explicitly rejected asparagus and leeks in the pot pie because they turn army-green and overcook by the time the sauce thickens and the crust browns. Stick with the longer-cooking vegetables: cremini mushrooms, sweet potato, turnip, and swiss chard. Cremini = baby bella; use those.

=== TOPPING VARIATION — PANKO INSTEAD OF PIE CRUST (PANKO PREFERRED OVER REGULAR BREADCRUMBS) ===

The pie can be topped with a crumb crust instead of the pie dough. When going this route, USE PANKO — not regular breadcrumbs. Panko's larger flakes crisp up into a distinct crunchy topping; regular breadcrumbs pack down against a wet vegetable filling and read soggy.

Scatter panko across the top of the filled pie plate, oil-spray or drizzle butter over the top so it browns properly, and bake uncovered until deeply golden. Similar pattern to [[dauphinois]] where breadcrumbs get oil-sprayed for the presentation crust.

Lighter and easier than the pie crust; skips the rolling/venting/egg-wash steps. The trade-off is you don't get the pastry structure — this is more of a gratin-style presentation than a proper pot pie.

=== VENT THE CRUST — FOUR 2-INCH OVAL VENTS IN THE CENTER ===

ATK's technique. The vents let steam out during the bake so the filling doesn't sog out the crust from below. Cutting the vents before you lay the crust on top (while it's still flat on parchment) is much easier than trying after.

=== SERVE AS A COMPLETE MEAL ===

Rich enough to be a main. The mushroom + sweet potato + turnip + chard combination covers the vegetable slot, the bouillon gravy carries the savory register, and the pastry provides the starch. A simple side salad with lemon vinaigrette is all it needs (or nothing at all).
original_chef: America's Test Kitchen — Vegetable Pot Pie (Hearty Vegetable Mains). Modifications: bouillon-based stock instead of vegetable broth, porcini mushroom powder instead of parmesan, fresh ginger added off heat as part of a lemon-and-ginger brightening axis (interchangeable or together), parsley skipped. Renamed 'turnip yam pie' to name the two roots that carry the dish.
